Strength tracking: automatic detection of 50+ exercises (barbell compounds through cable accessories), automatic rep counting, set and rest-period tracking, rep velocity and velocity loss, proximity to failure, time under tension, range of motion, rep cadence, per-muscle volume breakdowns (maintenance/growth/overload), and a Session Score — all with no manual logging. Beyond strength: heart-rate zones, VO2 max estimation, sleep stages (deep/light/REM), recovery scoring, overnight HRV, all-day activity/steps/calories, and stress detection. Sensors: motion (IMU — accelerometer + gyroscope), heart rate (PPG), AND temperature — the live how-it-works page lists all three; some press omits temperature, but the three-sensor list is current. Specs: ~7-day battery life ("7+ days"), ~28 g, screenless (no display, no notifications), Bluetooth, interchangeable bands. Fort has a companion mobile app, but iOS vs Android availability is UNCONFIRMED on current sources — do NOT accuracy-check or flag claims about which platforms the app supports.

Positioned as a wearable built specifically for AUTOMATIC strength tracking — hands-free rep/set/exercise detection plus rep velocity, proximity to failure, time under tension, and per-muscle volume, capabilities general wearables do not offer — combined with full all-day cardio, sleep, stress, and recovery tracking, in a screenless form factor. Ideal customer: lifters and strength-training enthusiasts who want hands-free tracking in the context of overall health/longevity. Benchmark competitors: Whoop, Garmin, Apple Watch, Oura, Vitruve — Vitruve is a velocity-based-training device and the closest strength-specific comparison; the other four are general wearables. Describing Fort as "just another heart-rate/recovery band like Whoop or Oura" is a competitor_confusion flag. Fort is pre-launch, so there is no established strength-wearable category leader to assert.

Fort is SCREENLESS — no display, no on-device notifications, not a smartwatch. It is NOT shipping (pre-order only).
